::: {.callout-note}
## About this page

- **What it is:** a briefing. Every claim here is drawn from the analyses on
  this site, from [How to Pull the Right
  Lever](https://adamdennett.github.io/school_attainment_tool/) and from the
  [Brighton and Hove school system
  model](https://adamdennett.github.io/bh-school-system/analysis.html). Each
  fact links to the page that computes it, so anything here can be checked.
- **Data:** published data only --- DfE, Ofsted and ONS. No pupil-level record
  is used anywhere. The one exception is noted on the school system model's own
  page.
- **Written to be argued with.** Where the evidence cuts against the way the
  city's schools are usually described --- in either direction --- that is said
  plainly. Section 10 lists what would change these conclusions.
- **Vintage:** the figures are as at the November 2026 build. Value added covers
  2021/22 to 2024/25; absence is full-year 2024/25 unless stated.
:::

## If you have five minutes {#sec-five-minutes}

1. **Brighton and Hove is a national success story on value added** --- 6th of 152
   local authorities --- and almost all of that is the city's schools holding
   up results against the worst absence in England.
2. **And yet its disadvantaged children leave school with Attainment 8 ranked
   122nd of 152** --- raw, with nothing allowed for. Bring absence alone to
   England's average and the city moves to about **69th**; allow for intake and
   context as well and its authority effect for those pupils is **18th of 151**.
   All of these are true at once, and the gap between them is mostly absence.
3. **Attainment 8 is not a measure of a good school - it's mainly a measure of who goes there.** Nationally it correlates with what a school actually adds at **0.27**,
   and intake alone predicts **81%** of it. The city needs to publish and lead on
   a value-added measure (I have developed one), particularly to change perceptions of schools like BACA.
4. **Absence is the biggest single lever in the city, and it is not poverty.**
   Disadvantage here is average; absence is the highest in England and rising.
5. **Children in the city's poorest neighbourhoods live further from a school than their better-off neighbours** --- almost uniquely in England. It traces back to the closure of CoMArt in 2005.
6. **The looming demographic crisis is locked in.** Year 7 falls by a fifth by 2032/33,
   and those children are already in the city's primary schools. Longhill has
   about 3.7 years of reserve. My new simulator can help us think of solutions. 
7. **Decline in children is driven by low fertility, not house prices keeping
   people out.** **0.98 children per woman in 2025 against England's 1.39** ---
   about 70% of the national rate --- and over 2023--25 the **joint
   second-lowest of 292 comparable districts**, level with Westminster and
   behind only Cambridge. Families do also leave, for Lewes, Mid Sussex and
   Wealden: that is **31st of 297 districts** on net child migration, and at
   **Year 7 it is about half the recent fall**.
8. **Social mixing is the weakest lever for narrowing the attainment gap the council has - and with additional travel could make it worse.** Attendance and fixing easy access to schools in the east will improve attainment and address the double disadvantage in the city.
9. **None of this needs new data collection.** I've been building tools on open data to assist with policy scenario testing - biggest barrier is awareness and open-mindedness.  

::: {.callout-important}
## The thread running through all of it

**The city is arguing about school quality using a number that is four-fifths
intake.** Attainment 8 tells you who a school admits; value added tells you what
it does with them. Nationally the two correlate at 0.27, and in Brighton and
Hove at 0.31 --- eight of the ten schools move four places or more between the
two tables.

Almost every mistake on this page follows from conflating the two. It is why the
city reads itself as 122nd when its schools are 18th
([section 2](#sec-disadvantaged)). It is why the school doing most for
disadvantaged children sits last in the published table and half empty
([section 3](#sec-measurement)). It is why social mixing looks like the lever
and attendance does not ([section 8](#sec-mixing)). And it is the one thing here
the council could change at no cost, with no consultation, by next admissions
round: **publish a value-added measure beside Attainment 8, and point families
at it.**
:::

---

## 1. The city is a national success story on value added {#sec-success}

Value Added v2.1 measures every state secondary in England against what its
intake and context predict: prior attainment, disadvantage, special educational
needs, pupil mobility, English as an additional language, school structure,
neighbourhood education and absence.

- **The city's ten secondaries average +1.4 Attainment 8 points against England.**
  Five are **significantly** above expectation --- their 95% intervals sit
  clear of zero --- and **none is significantly below**. Two do score below
  expectation (Longhill -1.5, Patcham -2.0), but both intervals still cross
  zero, Patcham's only barely (-4.0 to +0.1), so neither is distinguishable
  from the schools it is being compared with
  ([Brighton and Hove](areas/brighton_and_hove.qmd)).
- **The local authority's own effect is +3.7% of Attainment 8, the 6th largest of
  152 authorities.** It is +3.9% for disadvantaged pupils (18th of 151), +3.7%
  for non-disadvantaged (4th), +2.8% for girls (14th) and +4.5% for boys (4th).
  It is there for every group and in every year
  ([geographical effects](bh_effect.qmd)).
- **It is an absence effect, and it almost exactly cancels one.** Over the four
  fitted years the city's schools ran 10.9% absence against England's 9.0%. On
  the model's absence coefficient that difference lowers expected Attainment 8
  by 4.5%. The authority effect, +3.7%, gives nearly all of it back.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest version of this fact

The right sentence is **"the city's schools achieve about what similar intakes
achieve elsewhere in England, despite unusually high absence"** --- not "the
city's schools add more than others". Take absence out of the model and the
authority falls from 6th to 59th, an effect indistinguishable from zero. On
value added computed with **no allowance for absence at all**, the city's schools
average **-0.7 points, 102nd of 151 authorities**.

That is still a real and unusual finding. It is not a licence to stop worrying.
:::

### The "Brighton effect" is partly how educated the city is

- **Around the city's schools, 43.4% of adults hold a degree-level (level 4+)
  qualification, against 33.2% around England's schools** --- 25th of 152
  authorities, and 9 of the 10 schools sit above England's median school
  ([geographical effects](bh_effect.qmd)).
- Across the city as a whole, **44.5% of adults aged 16 and over hold a
  degree-level qualification against England's 33.8%** (Census 2021, TS067).
  Among South East **cities** that is second only to Oxford (48.1%), ahead of
  Bristol (42.1%), Reading (40.4%), Canterbury (33.1%), Southampton (31.6%) and
  Portsmouth (30.0%). Counting every South East district, including the affluent
  commuter districts, the city is 8th of 64 --- behind Elmbridge, Oxford,
  Waverley, Wokingham, Windsor and Maidenhead, Winchester and Woking.
- **The model already credits this, and cannot credit more.** Neighbourhood
  education lifts the city's expected Attainment 8 by about +1.1 points for all
  pupils, +1.3 for non-disadvantaged and only +0.3 for disadvantaged pupils. It
  accounts for about **32%** of what would otherwise look like a city effect.
  Drawing the neighbourhood more tightly (the 5, 10, 25, 50 or 100 nearest output
  areas, or distance-weighted) fits *worse* at every step and leaves the effect
  *larger*. The best-fitting version moves the city's effect only from +3.7% to
  +3.6%.
- **What the Census cannot see is the likeliest explanation of the rest.** The
  measure counts every adult, not parents --- students, whose highest
  qualification while studying is usually level 3, and young graduates with no
  school-age children both sit in it, pulling opposite ways. The leading reading
  of the leftover is **family resources that keep learning going when a child
  misses a day**: a parent who can help catch up, flexible or home-based work,
  tutoring, books. Free school meals does not see this, and neither, quite, does
  a Census count of all adults.

---

## 2. Its disadvantaged children still leave with poor results {#sec-disadvantaged}

This is the fact that should sit beside the one above, and it is the one most
often missing from the city's account of itself.

| Measure, 2024/25 | Brighton and Hove | England | Rank of 152 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attainment 8, all pupils | 45.5 | 46.8 | 85th |
| **Attainment 8, disadvantaged pupils** | **33.9** | **37.7** | **122nd** |
| Attainment 8, non-disadvantaged | 49.6 | 49.9 | 68th |
| **Disadvantage gap (points)** | **15.7** | **12.2** | **13th widest** |
| Disadvantaged (FSM6) % | 28.8 | 28.4 | 74th |

### What 122nd is, and what it is not {#sec-122nd}

**Every figure in the table above is raw.** It is the Attainment 8 the city's
disadvantaged pupils actually achieved, with no allowance for absence, intake or
anything else. That is the right number for asking *how are these children
doing?* --- and the wrong one for asking *how are these schools doing?* The two
questions have different answers, and the distance between them is mostly
absence.

| What is allowed for | Disadvantaged pupils' standing |
|---|---|
| **Nothing** --- raw Attainment 8 | 33.9 points, **122nd of 152** |
| **Absence only**, brought to England's average | 36.9 points, **69th** |
| **Intake, context and absence** --- the authority effect on v2.1 | +3.9%, **18th of 151** |
| *the same model with the absence term taken out* | *-0.0%, 78th of 151* |

Read the middle row first. If every Brighton and Hove school's absence fell to
England's school average of 8.6% in 2024/25 and **nothing else changed**, the
model puts its disadvantaged pupils' Attainment 8 up by **3.0 points on
average** --- and the city moves from **122nd to about 69th**. The gain is
concentrated where absence is worst: **+6.7 points at Brighton Aldridge, +6.2 at
Longhill, +5.3 at Hove Park**, and nothing at all at King's and Patcham, which
already run at or below the national rate.

**So absence is most of the shortfall, but not all of it.** Even with absence at
England's average the city would sit at 36.9 against England's 38.0 --- still
below, but a little over half a point rather than four points. What is left is
the region, the disadvantage gap itself, and special educational needs.

**The bottom two rows are the same point from the other end.** Once intake and
context *and* absence are allowed for, the city's authority effect for
disadvantaged pupils is +3.9%, 18th of 151. Strip just the absence term out of
that model and it collapses to -0.0%, 78th. Absence is what separates 18th from
78th.

::: {.callout-important}
## How to say this without overclaiming

**"Our disadvantaged children are 122nd of 152 on raw results, and on the
model's arithmetic absence accounts for most of that gap."** Not *"we would be
69th if absence were fixed"* as a prediction.

Three reasons. The middle row holds every other authority at today's absence, so
it is "if Brighton alone closed its absence gap", not a league table anyone will
ever see. The absence gradient is **associational**: it says what schools with
less absence look like once intake is accounted for, not what these schools would
gain by cutting absence by a given amount. And part of the gradient is
standing in for things absence travels with --- family stress, poverty beyond
free school meals, disengagement --- so some of that 3.0 points would not arrive
just because attendance improved.

What survives all three caveats is the direction and the order of magnitude: on
every way of cutting it, absence is the largest single thing standing between
the city's disadvantaged children and the results their intake predicts.
:::

### The level moves a long way. The gap moves less {#sec-level-not-gap}

Worth separating, because the national target is written in terms of the gap and
these two answers differ.

| If absence fell to England's average | Now | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disadvantaged pupils' Attainment 8 | 33.9 | 36.9 | **+3.0** |
| Non-disadvantaged pupils' Attainment 8 | 49.6 | 51.9 | +2.3 |
| **The disadvantage gap** | **15.7** | **15.0** | **-0.7** |
| Rank on the gap (1 = widest) | 13th | 22nd | |

- **The level is transformed: 122nd to 69th.** That is the number that matters
  for a child, and it is the case for treating absence as the city's
  first-order problem.
- **The gap narrows by only 0.7 points**, because better attendance lifts
  everyone. It closes about **19% of the 3.6 points by which the city's gap
  exceeds England's** --- real, but not the whole story.
- **Absence is still the most progressive lever available.** The gradient is
  **77% steeper for disadvantaged pupils**, so they gain 3.0 points against 2.3.
  Almost nothing else in the model helps them more than everyone else;
  neighbourhood education, for instance, is worth +2.6% to a non-disadvantaged
  pupil and +0.8% to a disadvantaged one ([section 8](#sec-mixing)).

**The honest conclusion, and the better argument.** A gap can be closed by the
top doing worse, and it tells you nothing about whether any child learned more.
The level tells you that. Absence is the largest lever on the level for the
city's poorest children by a wide margin, and a moderately progressive lever on
the gap as well. If the choice is between a policy that narrows the gap on paper
and one that raises disadvantaged children's results by three points, take the
three points.

- **The gap is the 13th widest in England** and three and a half points wider
  than England's.
- **The region makes it worse.** For disadvantaged pupils the South East is the
  **worst region in England**: -4.1% of Attainment 8 against England, while
  London is +5.1%. London's lead belongs to its disadvantaged pupils alone ---
  its non-disadvantaged pupils are at -1.5%
  ([geographical effects across England](geography.qmd)).
- **Place matters most for exactly the group policy most wants to help.** One
  standard deviation of local authority effect is worth 3.8% of Attainment 8 for
  disadvantaged pupils against 2.4% for non-disadvantaged; a region, 2.7% against
  1.6%.

---

## 3. Attainment 8 is not a measure of a good school --- and the whole debate runs on it {#sec-measurement}

This is the measurement error underneath every other argument in the city, and
it is the cheapest thing on this page to fix.

### Nationally, the headline score barely tells you what a school adds

- **Raw Attainment 8 and Value Added v2.1 correlate at 0.27** across England's
  3,265 state secondaries. The headline score accounts for about **7%** of what
  a school actually adds.
- **Intake and context alone predict 81% of the variation in a school's headline
  Attainment 8.** Four-fifths of the number published about a school is a
  description of the children who walked through the door.
- The spreads say the same thing. Headline Attainment 8 varies across schools
  with a standard deviation of **9.3 points**; value added, **2.6 points**. Most
  of what a league table displays is not the school.
- **So the headline number actively misleads, in both directions.** Of the
  schools in the top quarter on raw Attainment 8, **38% are below average on
  value added**. Of those in the bottom quarter, **28% are above average**. A
  parent choosing on the published score has close to a coin-flip's information
  about whether the school is any good at teaching.

### In Brighton and Hove the two tables are almost unrelated

The city's ten schools, ranked by the number families are pointed at, and by
what the schools add. Within the city the two correlate at **0.31**.

| School | Attainment 8 | Rank | Value added | Rank | Moves |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| King's School | 53.6 | 1st | +2.1 | 6th | **-5** |
| Dorothy Stringer | 53.2 | 2nd | +3.0 | 3rd | -1 |
| Blatchington Mill | 50.8 | 3rd | +1.2 | 7th | **-4** |
| Cardinal Newman | 50.3 | 4th | +0.6 | 8th | **-4** |
| Varndean | 48.8 | 5th | +3.1 | **1st** | **+4** |
| Patcham High | 45.5 | 6th | -2.0 | 10th | **-4** |
| Portslade Aldridge | 42.5 | 7th | +3.1 | **2nd** | **+5** |
| Hove Park | 41.0 | 8th | +2.6 | 4th | **+4** |
| Brighton Aldridge | 36.1 | 9th | +2.2 | 5th | **+4** |
| Longhill High | 32.9 | 10th | -1.5 | 9th | +1 |

- **Eight of the ten schools move four places or more.** The school families are
  told is best is 6th on what it adds; the 7th-placed school is 2nd.
- **Longhill is 20.7 Attainment 8 points below the city's highest, and 4.6 points
  below the best on value added.** Most of what separates it from the popular
  schools is its intake, not its teaching.
- **Brighton Aldridge is last of the ten on the headline score and 5th on value
  added** --- while doing more for disadvantaged pupils than any school in the
  city ([section 8](#sec-mixing)).

### And it is the same error the city makes about itself

[Section 2](#sec-disadvantaged) is this error at city scale. Brighton and Hove is
**122nd of 152** on raw disadvantaged Attainment 8 and **18th of 151** once
intake, context and absence are allowed for. Both numbers describe the same
schools in the same year. Which one you quote decides whether the city looks
like a failure or a success, and only one of them is about the schools.

### The loop this creates, and who pays for it

The council writes the admissions guide, and it tells parents to look at each
school's exam results and Ofsted reports. Families do as advised: **headline
Attainment 8 explains 84% of how heavily each school is preferred, and value
added 20%**. Each point of headline score goes with about **7% more preferences
per place**.

That advice is self-defeating, and it runs in one direction only:

> a school with a more disadvantaged intake posts a lower headline score →
> it is chosen less → its roll shrinks and its intake becomes more
> disadvantaged → its headline score falls again.

**The schools the published number punishes are precisely the ones doing most
for the city's poorest children.** Brighton Aldridge is the clearest case in
England-wide terms, and it is the school the headline table puts last.

### What changing the number would be worth

Run the city's school system model with families reading the four-year value
added measure as closely as they now read the headline score --- same places,
same catchments, same rules, same journeys, only the number families are taken
to be reading changes:

- **Brighton Aldridge goes from 90 children to 174 on 180 places: half empty to
  97% full.** Hove Park and Portslade Aldridge fill.
- **The share of the city's empty Year 7 places sitting in just three schools
  falls from 93% to 75%** --- the difference between a surplus that is a
  budgeting problem and one that is a viability problem
  ([section 6](#sec-demographics)).
- Mean journeys shorten, and deprived children's extra travel falls from 3.5 to
  2.6 minutes each way.
- **It creates no places and removes none.** What changes is which schools are
  empty.

It is the largest single change modelled anywhere in this work, it costs
nothing, and it needs no consultation --- only a different sentence in a guide
the council already publishes, and a contextualised measure printed beside the
headline one. **That measure exists**: it is on this site, for every state
secondary in England.

::: {.callout-important}
## The one-sentence version

**Attainment 8 measures who a school admits; value added measures what it does
with them.** Parents, councillors and campaigners are arguing about school
quality using a number that is four-fifths intake --- and the city's own
admissions guide is what points them at it. Publish both, and lead with the one
that is about the school.
:::

---

## 4. Absence is the biggest lever, and it is not poverty {#sec-absence}

### How bad it is

- **11.3% overall absence in 2024/25 --- the highest of 152 local authorities**
  on the v2.1 school frame, and the second highest on the frame used in *How to
  Pull the Right Lever*. Either way, the top of the table.
- **And getting worse.** The city was 9th in 2021/22, 17th in 2022/23, 10th in
  2023/24, 1st in 2024/25.
- **Persistent absence 30.6%, 4th of 152** (England 23.9%).
- **Disadvantaged pupils' absence 18.0% against England's 13.2%**, 3rd of 150
  authorities (DfE, absence by pupil characteristics).
- Severe absence --- missing half of schooling or more --- runs **52% above
  England's average school**, and 11% above even after intake is allowed for.

### Why it is not poverty

- **Disadvantage in the city is average**: FSM6 28.8% against England's 28.4%,
  74th of 152. Mean prior attainment (KS2) is 50th of 152.
- **Suspensions are low**: 13.0 episodes per 100 pupils against England's 21.2;
  5.9 pupils per 100 suspended at least once against 7.3. This is not a
  discipline problem.
- **It is above what the intake predicts.** On the v2.1 intake terms the city's
  schools ran **+1.7 percentage points above the absence their pupils' profiles
  predict --- 3rd highest of 152 authorities**. Of the 2.7-point gap with
  England, about 1.7 points is not explained by who lives here.
- **Seven of the ten schools run more than a point above their predicted
  absence.** Longhill is +4.2, Brighton Aldridge +3.7, Blatchington Mill +2.3.
  Only King's runs more than a point below.

### What kind of absence

| Measure (% of sessions, 2021/22–2024/25) | Brighton and Hove | England | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| All absence | 10.9 | 9.0 | +1.9 |
| **Illness (authorised)** | **5.7** | **4.3** | **+1.4** |
| Unauthorised | 3.2 | 3.0 | +0.3 |
| Other authorised | 1.5 | 1.3 | +0.2 |

- **Of the 1.9 points of extra absence, 1.4 is authorised illness.**
  Unauthorised absence is close to England's.
- After intake is allowed for, the city's **illness** effect is **+27%, 2nd of
  152 authorities**; its **unauthorised** effect is **-5%, 110th**
  ([what goes with absence](absence_causes.qmd)).
- This is where the interesting question sits. Authorised illness may include
  anxiety and health-related absence that behaves differently from
  disengagement; it may also reflect how the city's schools code and authorise
  absence. School-level data cannot separate those two, and
  [the geographical effects page](bh_effect.qmd#what-would-help-tell-them-apart) lists the published tables
  that would.

### What it costs, and what it is worth

- **11.3% against England's 8.6% is worth about -2.8 Attainment 8 points** for
  all pupils, **-3.2 for disadvantaged pupils** and -2.4 for non-disadvantaged.
  The gradient is **77% steeper for disadvantaged pupils**.
- **Cutting a school's absence by a tenth goes with Attainment 8 2.5% higher for
  all pupils, 3.5% for disadvantaged pupils and 1.9% for non-disadvantaged.**
  Absence is the only large lever in the model that *narrows* the gap
  ([the simulator](simulator.qmd)).
- Indicatively, if each school's absence fell to England's 8.6%: Longhill +5.5
  Attainment 8 points for all pupils and **+6.2 for disadvantaged pupils**;
  Brighton Aldridge +5.1 and +6.7; Hove Park +4.6 and +5.3.
- **Being an exceptional school buys back only about half of what high absence
  costs.** Nationally, moving an average school's absence to where the highest 5%
  of schools sit costs about 4.5 Attainment 8 points; being a top-decile school
  on value added gains about 2.3 back ([home](index.qmd#sec-add-take)).

### The national picture, for context

- England's autumn-and-spring absence rose from **5.2% of sessions in 2018/19 to
  8.7% in 2022/23** and has eased only to **8.0% in 2025/26**. Illness has come
  most of the way back; unauthorised and other authorised absence have not.
  **Severe absence has risen from 1.2% of pupils to 3.6%** and is still near its
  peak ([how absence changes](absence_change.qmd)).
- **Absence is sticky.** Once the national swing is removed, 66% of the variation
  in overall absence is a school's lasting level. Of the fifth of schools with
  the highest unauthorised absence before the pandemic, 62% are still in the top
  fifth now. But more than a third are not: it moves.

---

## 5. Disadvantaged children here travel furthest --- almost uniquely in England {#sec-distance}

- **Across England, children in deprived neighbourhoods usually live *closer* to
  a secondary school.** That holds in cities, towns and the countryside, and in
  **81% of the 293 districts**.
- **Brighton and Hove is the other way round.** Children in the most deprived
  third of its neighbourhoods live **1.57 km** from their nearest school; the
  rest live **1.18 km**. That is **33% further** --- the **5th largest difference
  of 293 districts** proportionately and the **2nd largest in kilometres**
  ([distance to school](distance.qmd)).
- **Among the 109 mostly urban local authorities, none has its deprived
  neighbourhoods further from a school.**

### On real streets and bus timetables

- By walking and bus, children in the city's most deprived neighbourhoods are
  **4.7 minutes further from a school than the rest**, and **9.0 minutes**
  further walking. **No comparator place is more than 1.3 minutes further**, and
  among all 109 mostly urban authorities the next largest gaps are Tameside
  (3.7) and Derby (3.4).
- **18% of those journeys need two or more buses --- the most of any authority in
  England.**
- From Whitehawk, the typical journey is **two buses across the city: about 39
  minutes to the quickest school and 44 to Dorothy Stringer**, both changing in
  the city centre. In Bristol, Southampton and Plymouth a typical deprived
  neighbourhood's journey is a walk or one short bus ride, 15 to 20 minutes.
- **29 of the city's 179 neighbourhoods --- about 385 cohort-aged children ---
  can reach no secondary school place at all within 30 minutes** by walking and
  bus on a weekday morning. Not their catchment school; any school.
- **Access and child poverty line up**, and in the wrong direction: they
  correlate at -0.33, and **25 neighbourhoods (about 400 children) sit in the
  least accessible third and the most deprived third at once** --- against only
  11 in the most deprived third and the best-served third
  ([the school system model, §4](https://adamdennett.github.io/bh-school-system/analysis.html)).

### It traces to 2005

- The city allocates by catchment with a lottery tie-break --- very unusual in
  England --- and that arrangement **dates from the closure of CoMArt in the east
  of the city in 2005** and the catchment system that replaced distance-based
  allocation in 2008. The shape of the system is still partly the shape of that
  closure.
- **A school back on CoMArt's old site would bring the deprived third to 1.19 km
  and close most of the gap** (the city would fall from 5th to 27th of 293
  districts). Longhill moved to the top of Elm Grove does much the same: 1.21 km,
  37th. On the city's school system model, **CoMArt reopened would cut
  disadvantaged children's journeys by 2.1 minutes**.

### How firm the link with absence is

Stated carefully, because the number is easy to over-read.

- Across 150 authorities and six years from 2018/19, **disadvantaged pupils'
  absence is 3.5 points higher for each extra kilometre** between deprived
  neighbourhoods and a school, against 0.6 for non-disadvantaged pupils. It
  holds on eleven measures of distance and is far weaker in primary schools, as
  it should be if the journey to secondary school is what matters.
- **But most of that slope is who lives in those places, not the journey.** Given
  the ethnic mix of disadvantaged pupils in each authority it falls to 0.6, and
  with every control to 0.3, with an interval including zero.
- **A smaller link survives three separate tests.** In mostly urban authorities
  outside London, 2.5 points per kilometre given ethnic mix and region, against
  0.4 in primary. Within one authority, 0.45 points per kilometre for pupils in
  the most deprived neighbourhoods. And each doubling of how far a school's
  nearest children live goes with 0.26 points more absence in every year. Across
  the 109 routed authorities, 1.9 points per kilometre with every control (2.5
  outside London).
- **Carried to GCSE results, it is an "if".** If the extra absence is caused by
  the journey, each kilometre would cost disadvantaged pupils about 2.2 to 2.7
  Attainment 8 points, and the city's gap about **1 point**. Attainment 8
  modelled directly shows no such effect, so this is a plausible upper bound,
  not a measured one.

---

## 6. The demographic crisis is locked in {#sec-demographics}

**The children who will enter Year 7 in 2033 are already in the city's primary
schools.** Their number is a count, not a forecast.

- **Reception is already down 20.4% since 2018/19**, primary-age pupils down
  13.7%, and the city is classed as in **consistent decline**
  ([pupil numbers and school places](demographics.qmd)).
- **Year 7 falls from 2,284 now to about 1,825 in 2032/33 --- a fall of 20%, the
  9th steepest of 159 areas in England.** The secondary roll falls 10.4% by
  2029/30.
- On the school system model, that implies something like **765 surplus Year 7
  places by 2033 --- two and a half average secondary schools' worth** --- and
  **93% of the city's empty Year 7 places currently sit in just three schools**.
  That is the difference between a budgeting problem and a viability problem.

### Longhill is the school with a deadline

| Year | Roll | Income/pupil | Spend/pupil | In-year balance | Reserve |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021-22 | 908 | £7,644 | £6,980 | +£602,810 | £960,852 |
| 2022-23 | 875 | £7,978 | £7,998 | -£17,469 | £943,383 |
| 2023-24 | 825 | £8,748 | £9,041 | -£243,505 | £699,878 |
| 2024-25 | **723** | £10,358 | £10,591 | -£168,435 | **£531,443** |

- **The roll has fallen from 908 to 723 in four years**, putting it in the bottom
  sixth of English secondaries by size. Per-pupil income rose --- the funding
  system working as intended --- and per-pupil spending rose faster.
- **At the recent rate of depletion, about £143,000 a year, the reserve supports
  roughly 3.7 more years.** That makes this a decision with a deadline rather
  than one that can be deferred to a consultation cycle.
- Longhill also carries the city's **highest absence (16.8%)**, **highest
  persistent absence (48%)**, **lowest value added (-1.5)**, **highest FSM
  (40.1%)** and a June 2026 report card of *Needs attention* on achievement and
  on curriculum and teaching. Its roll and its absence are the same story told
  twice.

### But the money is not only a Longhill problem

- **45% of the city's 47 maintained schools were in deficit in 2025-26**, against
  21% across England and 17% in the South East --- **9th highest of 129
  authorities**. The peak was **58% in 2024-25, the highest of 129 authorities
  that year** ([Brighton and Hove: school finances](finance_areas/brighton_and_hove.qmd)).
- Together they hold a **net deficit of £3.0m**, against net reserves of £7.8m in
  2021-22. The typical maintained school's reserve is **0.2% of a year's income**
  against England's 5.6%.
- **Eight open schools sit in the early-warning band and five show three or more
  warning signs** --- the most of any Sussex district.
- **Nine of the ten secondaries have been spending reserves, and the two deepest
  deficits are not Longhill** --- they are Hove Park and Cardinal Newman, one of
  them the largest school in the city.

### The national pattern this sits in

- England's primary-age pupils peaked in 2018/19 and are **5.3% down by 2025/26**;
  Year 7 will be about **10% smaller in 2032/33**, and 15% or more smaller in 28
  areas.
- **Rolls fall first and money follows.** Of the 241 primary schools that closed
  or merged from 2017/18, the typical one had lost 23% of its pupils by the year
  before closing and was 63% full against 93% for schools that stayed open. Its
  reserves only slipped in the last two or three years: **by the time the deficit
  shows, the pupils have gone** ([school finances before closure](finance.qmd)).
- A simple early-warning model on published returns picks this up: trained on
  closures to 2020/21, **the riskiest 5% of returns contained 69% of the schools
  that closed in the test years** (AUC 0.92). Falling rolls carry most of the
  warning.
- **Closures have followed falling rolls in inner London and almost nowhere
  else.** Most falling areas carry surplus places instead. Outside London,
  Brighton and Hove is among the areas that have closed most for their size.

---

## 7. It is fertility --- not families leaving, and not house prices {#sec-fertility}

- **The city's total fertility rate is 0.98 children per woman (2025) against
  England's 1.39** --- about 70% of the national rate.
- **On the steadier three-year average (2023--25) it is 0.97, the joint
  second-lowest of 292 comparable districts**, level with Westminster and behind
  only Cambridge (0.92). Worth quoting on this basis rather than on one year: a
  single year moves, and the three-year figure is what the analysis ranks.
  On 2025 alone the city is 5th of all 318 districts, behind Cambridge,
  Islington, Westminster and the City of London.
- **Births fell from 2,952 in 2015 to about 2,100 a year since 2022.**

### Births, not migration

Splitting the change in pupils exactly into births, migration since birth, and
the share of children in state mainstream schools:

- **Primary pupils fell 14% from 2018/19 to 2025/26, and births account for all
  of it** (-18.6 on the log scale ×100). Migration (+2.5) and the state-school
  share (+1.4) slightly *offset* it.
- **The city does lose children** --- about **92% of each birth cohort is still
  living there at primary age, against England's 105%** --- but that loss is
  long-standing. **It explains the low level, not the fall.**
- For comparison, in the median London borough primary pupils fell 12.1, split
  roughly half births and half families leaving. Brighton and Hove is not that
  story.

### Where the city sits on child migration {#sec-child-migration}

- **It is in the losing minority, and near the wrong end of it.** Net migration
  of children aged 0--10 runs at **-4.7 per 1,000 a year (2019--25): 31st of 297
  districts**. Only **45 of the 297 lose children at all**, and the median
  district *gains* **14 per 1,000**.
- **It is the UK, not abroad.** Within the UK the city loses **12.1 per 1,000**;
  from abroad it gains **7.4**, which cancels more than half of it. Adults aged
  30--39 behave the same way: **-14.6** internal, **+11.9** international.
- **They move next door.** Lewes gains **19.6** children per 1,000 a year, Mid
  Sussex **25.5** and Wealden **33.5** --- the same districts with much the same
  house prices and fertility half again as high
  ([the fertility model](#sec-fertility)).
- **But the loss is mild by city standards and it is easing.** Lambeth loses
  **43** per 1,000, Wandsworth 42, Hackney 36. And the city's own net loss has
  roughly halved, from **-12.9 in 2013--18 to -4.7 in 2019--25**. A loss that is
  shrinking cannot be what made the rolls fall.

::: {.callout-note}
## One qualification, and it matters for secondary schools

The "births, not migration" split holds for primary, and for the city's
*shortage* of children overall. **It does not hold for Year 7.** On the same
decomposition, the 2018 to 2025 fall in Year 7 was **-7.1 in total: births -4.4
and migration -5.1**, so migration was the *larger* half, and the city ranks
**33rd of 148 areas** on that term (the median area is +2.1). The reason is
retention: the share of a birth cohort still living in the city at age 11 fell
from **92% to 87%**.

So the honest division is: **the city has few children because of fertility, and
its secondary rolls are falling for both reasons about equally.** For primary
planning, births are the story. For secondary planning --- which is what the
rest of this page is about --- families leaving before Year 7 is doing as much
work as the birth rate, and it is the half a council could in principle
influence.
:::

### House prices explain little

- Across districts, **the house price to earnings ratio accounts for 7% of the
  differences in fertility. Women's education alone accounts for 27%.** A
  five-measure model --- women's education, the share of women in their early
  twenties, partnership, private renting and birthplace --- reaches **67%**.
- **The city sits 0.44 children per woman below what its house-price ratio alone
  predicts, the 2nd largest gap in England.** Add the other four measures and the
  gap disappears entirely (residual +0.01).
- **Brighton and Hove's gap with the average district, by measure:** a young,
  largely student population -0.13; highly educated women -0.13; few married or
  civil partnered couples -0.14 (274th of 288); private renting -0.10; house
  prices themselves **-0.06**. Housing, through renting and prices together, is
  about a third of the gap.
- **The neighbours are the test.** Lewes, Mid Sussex and Wealden have house price
  to earnings ratios of 10.1 to 10.7 against the city's 10.6 to 11.1 --- and
  fertility of **1.45 to 1.58**.
- **The fall itself is national.** The city fell 0.41 children per woman; the
  typical English district fell 0.39. **Where housing became less affordable,
  fertility fell no more than where it did not.** Nothing local explains the
  fall in any district: within districts over time, local changes explain about
  half of one per cent of the movement.
- **One genuinely unusual feature.** In 97% of districts most of the fall came
  from mothers under 30, which is consistent with births being postponed. In
  Brighton and Hove, Cambridge and Oxford it splits evenly --- -0.21 under 30 and
  -0.20 at 30 and over. In these cities later births have **not** made up for
  fewer early ones.
- **Within the city the shortfall is central.** Brunswick and the North Laine
  have 47 under-fives per 1,000 adults aged 20 to 44, against the city's 122 and
  England's 172; Mile Oak, Hangleton North and Portslade by Sea are at or above
  England's. **22% of the city's output areas have fewer than 60**, against 5%
  across England. Neighbourhood make-up accounts for almost all of it.
- **But do not read that map as a list of schools to shrink.** Across England and
  within the city, primaries in low-child areas have **not** lost Reception
  pupils faster than others. The council's own forecasts leave the **most
  unfilled places in the outer planning areas** --- The Deans 63%, West
  Blatchington and North Hangleton 59%, Portslade 43% --- which have plenty of
  young children ([note for the council](bh_births_note.qmd)).

---

## 8. Social mixing is the weakest lever available {#sec-mixing}

This section is the one that most directly contradicts recent policy, so it is
set out with the arithmetic.

### How much a school can reach at all

- Sixty years of school-effectiveness research puts the share of variation in
  outcomes attributable to schools rather than to their intakes at **8 to 15 per
  cent**. Decomposing the multilevel model lands in the same place: **a school
  can reach about 12% of the variance in its results**, against roughly **42%
  that arrives with the intake**.
- **Almost all of that reachable 12% runs through attendance.** The workforce a
  school hires accounts for about **2.5%** of the variance for all pupils and
  **0.8% for disadvantaged pupils**; the school-controllable half of absence
  accounts for **9%** and **11.7%** respectively --- fourteen times larger for
  the group the policy is aimed at.
- **Moving children between schools touches neither term.** It changes which
  building a child attends without changing their attendance or their
  circumstances.
- Nationally, absence explains **56%** of the variation in school-level
  Attainment 8 and prior attainment 50%, while deprivation explains **21%**.

### Disadvantaged pupils do not do worse where they are concentrated

- **Given their prior attainment, disadvantaged pupils do slightly *better* where
  more of their schoolmates are disadvantaged** --- an elasticity of +0.027
  (t = 7.0) in their own model. The effect is small, and it appears to run
  through schools organised to serve those pupils rather than through
  concentration itself.
- **Disadvantaged pupils' value added does not rise with the school's
  neighbourhood education.** Across England the two correlate at 0.12, but that is
  London; outside London it is **-0.05**, and within local authorities **-0.02**.
- **Schools in more educated neighbourhoods have *wider* gaps, not narrower.**
  Outside London the gap between non-disadvantaged and disadvantaged pupils rises
  from **10.9 points in the least educated fifth of neighbourhoods to 14.9 in the
  most**. Each standard deviation of neighbourhood education widens it by 1.0
  point (t = 11).
- **A standard deviation of neighbourhood education is worth +0.8% of Attainment
  8 to a disadvantaged pupil, against +2.6% to a non-disadvantaged one.** The
  thing being redistributed is worth little to the children it is being
  redistributed for.
- **And the city's schools are already relatively mixed:** 47th least segregated
  of 152 authorities on Gorard's index in 2024/25 (0.129 against a median of
  0.145). Adding local segregation to the value added model changes the city's
  authority effect **not at all** (+3.7% against +3.7%).

### BACA is the local proof

Brighton Aldridge Community Academy has the most disadvantaged intake in the city
(FSM 52.6%), the city's highest absence after Longhill, and about 30% of pupils
arriving with low prior attainment.

- **Value added +2.2 points for all pupils, +2.4 for disadvantaged pupils and
  +2.6 for non-disadvantaged** --- above expectation for both groups, with a gap
  of only +0.2. On the earlier panel model a disadvantaged pupil leaving BACA in
  2024/25 did about **5.7 Attainment 8 points better than a comparable pupil at a
  similar school elsewhere in England**, and 3.1 points better averaged over four
  years.
- Ofsted rated it **Good in every area in April 2025**.
- That is far larger than the fraction of a point any redistribution of pupils
  could deliver.
- Portslade Aldridge tells a similar story: +3.1 points overall, the joint
  strongest in the city.

### What the city's admissions changes actually did

On the city's own school system model, run on its published settings:

- **The 2024 catchment map lengthened disadvantaged children's journeys by about
  0.3 minutes**, and priority 6 by another 0.06 --- against a **4.7-minute gap**
  that comes from where the schools are, not from the rules.
- **Mixing moved by 0.011 on the model's index, about 9% of the segregation
  before it** --- and the model itself warns that differences of a few thousandths
  are inside what a change of measure has moved.
- In Attainment 8 points, that is a journey cost of about **0.06** against a
  generous mixing gain of up to **0.20**. Both are a fraction of a point.

**But the city average hides Whitehawk.**

- The six zones moved **out of Longhill's catchment and into Dorothy Stringer's
  and Varndean's** are in Whitehawk and the edge of Roedean and Marina: about
  **78 children a year, 59 of them disadvantaged**, in neighbourhoods with an
  IDACI score of **0.43 against 0.14** for the zones the map left alone.
- Their journeys, already among the longest in the city, **lengthened by 3.1
  minutes on average to 57, and by 4.5 minutes to 56 for the disadvantaged
  children among them**. The share offered Longhill fell from **22% to 5%**.
- On the chain, that is up to about **0.7 Attainment 8 points each** --- ten times
  the city average, for the city's poorest children.
- Putting Whitehawk back would shorten disadvantaged children's journeys by 0.5
  minutes and raise the segregation index by 0.015.

### The proposals that did not go ahead would have been worse

The council first proposed priority 6 at 20% with Dorothy Stringer and
Blatchington Mill each cut from 330 places to 300. Class Divide argued for 30%
with the same cuts. Neither had a published model run, so both were run here on
the published model.

| Run | Disadv. journey (min) | Other children (min) | Displaced | Segregation index | Priority 6 places |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Today (priority 6 at 5%) | 32.12 | 28.66 | 6 | 0.116 | 69 |
| Priority 6 at 20% | 32.24 | 28.81 | 14 | 0.124 | 117 |
| The council's proposal: both | 32.35 | 29.21 | **40** | 0.117 | 117 |
| Class Divide: 30% and the cuts | 32.35 | 29.21 | **40** | 0.117 | 117 |

- **Children without a place at their catchment school would have risen from 6 to
  40.** Journeys would have lengthened for disadvantaged children (+0.23 minutes)
  and more for everyone else (+0.55).
- **And intakes would have been no more mixed.** Priority 6 at 20% on its own
  *raises* the index to 0.124; the cuts lower it a little; together they leave it
  at 0.117, where it is today.
- **Above about 15%, priority 6 does nothing, because demand runs out.** 69
  places are taken at 5%, 108 at 10%, and **117 from 20% on, and no more**. So
  Class Divide's 30% would have done exactly what the council's 20% did --- and
  so would 40%.
- **By 2030 the cuts would not bite at all**, because both schools will fill
  fewer than 300 places anyway.
- The children whose journeys would have lengthened most live in Hollingbury,
  Fiveways and West Blatchington --- **among the least deprived neighbourhoods in
  the city** --- displaced from full schools. Longhill's catchment would have
  gained nothing.

::: {.callout-note}
## What this does not say

It does not say schools do not matter: a persistent school effect of 15.6% across
3,500 secondaries is a great deal, and the city's schools mostly perform above
what their intakes predict. Nor does it say segregation between schools is
acceptable --- there are fairness arguments for mixed intakes that have nothing
to do with attainment. The claim is narrower and harder to argue with: **the
council should not expect a redistribution policy to move attainment much,
because the mechanism it works through is the smallest term available.** And this
is school-level evidence, which cannot isolate what one pupil would gain by
moving.
:::

---

## 9. Four things that would help {#sec-what-would-help}

In rough order of how much they would move, per pound and per year of political
capital spent. The first is free; the second is the largest lever on results.

### 1. Publish a value-added measure, and point families at it

**The cheapest large change available: no money, no consultation, and it could
be in the next admissions guide.** The evidence is in
[section 3](#sec-measurement); the action is three things.

- **Change the sentence in the admissions guide.** It currently sends parents to
  each school's exam results and Ofsted reports --- the numbers that are
  four-fifths intake.
- **Print a contextualised measure beside Attainment 8** wherever the council
  publishes school results. One exists for every state secondary in England,
  on this site, built from published data and free to reuse.
- **Use it in the council's own papers.** Consultation documents, scrutiny
  reports and the case made for or against any individual school currently lean
  on the headline figure, which is the number least able to bear the weight.

On the city's model this is the **largest single change modelled anywhere in
this work**: Brighton Aldridge from 90 children to 174 on 180 places, the
concentration of empty Year 7 places in three schools falling from 93% to 75%,
and deprived children's journeys shortening --- without creating or removing a
single place.

It will not raise anyone's results by itself. It stops the city actively
misdirecting families, and it stops the self-fulfilling loop that empties the
schools doing most for its poorest children.

### 2. Attendance, treated as the city's first-order problem

The largest lever in the model and the only large one that narrows the gap: 3.5%
of Attainment 8 per 10% cut in absence for disadvantaged pupils, against 1.9%
for others. About half of a school's absence is structural and about half is not.
The city's extra absence is mostly authorised illness, which is where the enquiry
should start --- including the question of how it is recorded.

The published tables that would sharpen this are listed on the
[geographical effects page](bh_effect.qmd#what-would-help-tell-them-apart): absence by pupil characteristics by authority
(is the city's extra absence among FSM pupils or not, and in which year groups?),
persistent absence and reasons over time, elective home education and children
missing education, and attainment by prior-attainment band.

### 3. A school children in the east can actually get to

A smaller Longhill at the top of Elm Grove, with the catchments redrawn around
it, is the option that does most for access **and** most for Longhill's roll:

- neighbourhoods reaching **no** place within 30 minutes falls from **29 to 15**
  --- **145 children** gain a reachable school place;
- places reachable within half an hour rises from 452 to 482 for the average
  child, and the journey to the nearest school falls by a minute;
- the gap between deprived children's journeys and everyone else's falls from
  **3.9 minutes to 0.4**;
- **Whitehawk's disadvantaged children's journeys fall from 57 minutes to 23**;
- Longhill takes 106 children in 2026 and 86 in 2030 at 150 places, against 89
  and 70 today;
- 153 of 179 neighbourhoods are better off and 26 --- the far south east --- are
  worse.

It **raises** the segregation index, from 0.111 to 0.151. That counts against it
under the council's stated aim of evening out intakes. On the evidence about
disadvantaged pupils' outcomes in section 8, it is not a cost to those pupils. A
review of how to even out disadvantaged children's chances has to choose between
those two measures, and should do so knowing both halves. It also does not make
Longhill break even --- about £0.7m a year at Elm Grove in 2030, £0.9m at
Ovingdean --- and that gap should go to members as the price of keeping a school
in the east.

### 4. Treat the bus network as an admissions instrument

The only lever here that widens real choice **without taking anything from
anyone**. 29 neighbourhoods can reach no place in half an hour, concentrated in
the more deprived third of the city. A bus timetable can change that; a catchment
boundary cannot.

One worked case: a child near a stop on the Whitehawk-to-Longhill school buses
(the 72 and 72A, three trips each way) who **misses the last workable journey
arrives about 17 minutes late**, against 0 to a few minutes at the other city
schools; walking would take about 70 minutes. Longhill also has the city's
highest absence. Across England this is **a striking case, not a pattern** ---
the correlation between the penalty and absence is near zero nationally --- so it
is a reason to look at Longhill, not a general law.

---

## 10. The evidence, and the gap in it {#sec-evidence}

### What has been published, and when

Everything above comes from published data. The analysis behind it has been
public since *How to Pull the Right Lever*, and the city's school system model,
its simulator and this site are all open, with code.

- **Absence was not part of the policy conversation.** It was not mentioned in
  the public engagement slides or the published materials for the 2024 admissions
  consultation, nor for the 2025 one --- in a city with the worst or second worst
  absence in England and near-average disadvantage.
- **The free school meals priority cannot yet be reviewed on outcomes, in either
  direction.** It took effect for entry in September 2023. Those children sit
  GCSEs in **summer 2028**. Not one cohort admitted under the policy has reached
  an examination.
- **And a single year of disadvantaged results is not evidence about a school.**
  For disadvantaged pupils, year-to-year noise (3.6 Attainment 8 points) is
  *larger* than the persistent difference between schools (2.7 points). **Two
  schools doing genuinely equally well by their disadvantaged pupils will differ
  by around 5 points in a given year for no reason at all** --- larger than most
  of the gaps that get argued about. Three years averaged, or it is mostly noise.

### Ten tables that would settle most of what is open

None requires new collection. All are aggregates the council already holds. The
full list is in the school system model
([§10.3](https://adamdennett.github.io/bh-school-system/analysis.html)); the
first five:

1. home LSOA of every applicant, by year and allocated school;
2. the full preference ordering, anonymised, by year;
3. allocated school by home LSOA, including schools outside the city;
4. the criterion under which each place was allocated;
5. children allocated a school they did not name, by school, year and home
   catchment.

**One of these has in effect already happened.** Appendix 1 of the council's
Educational Equity Framework counts Key Stage 2 and Key Stage 4 pupils by ward
and MSOA, as a by-product of describing attainment. Those counts gave the model's
origins their first external check: the geography holds, correlating at 0.96. But
the council's own place planning applies **a single state-sector share of 0.85
city-wide**, where the real range runs from about **0.66 in Round Hill to 1.21 in
Woodingdean** --- enough to change which schools look full. A table published for
another purpose answered a question that had been described as unanswerable.

### What would change these conclusions

- **The firmest findings are the demographic ones**: they are counts of children
  already in school, adjusted by a transfer rate that has moved under two
  percentage points in a decade.
- **The accessibility findings are firm in direction and approximate in
  magnitude**: modelled journey times, not measured ones.
- **The value added and absence findings are associations between schools**, not
  effects on pupils. The absence gradient says what schools with more absence
  look like once intake is accounted for, not what one school would gain by
  cutting absence by a given amount. Direction and order of magnitude are what to
  take from them.
- **The school system model's results are the softest**: swept rather than
  calibrated, because calibration needs the tables above. Every comparison is
  robust across the swept range; no single number is a prediction.
